numerical_claim_candidates.text: - Register compression of the model's visible replies is the only style lever worth real money: locally measured **−54% to −67%** tokens on instruction/reply ladders (Fable tokenizer, method below), consistent with baseline's session-level **caveman-ultra = 58.5%** (its "~75%" marketing claim is character-level folklore). On the modeled session profile that is **~10% of session dollars, hard-capped at 17%** even at total muteness.
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Withdrawn as current workload evidence: original complete session fixture and current usage receipts not reproduced; no universal thinking or visible-output ceiling.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: - The cap exists because **thinking = 54.8% of output tokens** (local, n=1), billed in full even when displayed summarized ("You're charged for the full thinking tokens... not the summary tokens" — live docs), and no style instruction reaches it. The documented lever past the cap is the **effort parameter** — and, correcting folklore, **NOT `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS`, which live docs say has no effect on Fable 5**.
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Reassessed under the mapped section; old number is not retained as current local measurement without the original complete fixture.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: - The reasoning-compression literature converges on the same band for visible CoT: CCoT **−48.70%** (FLLM 2024), TALE **−67%** with <3pp accuracy loss, Chain of Draft to **7.6–21% of CoT tokens**, Sketch-of-Thought **up to −84%** (EMNLP 2025) — all measured on QA benchmarks, none on agentic coding, none on adaptive thinking.
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Reassessed under the mapped section; old number is not retained as current local measurement without the original complete fixture.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: - Glyph/symbol prompt DSLs are **anti-recommended on Claude**: telegraphic ASCII English beat a SynthLang-style prompt by ~26% in two independent local samples; exotic glyphs cost **3.9–4.9 tokens each**; the one comprehension study found Claude Haiku 4.5 parses symbolic instructions at 100% but obeys operators at **26% fidelity** (silent disobedience).
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Reassessed under the mapped section; old number is not retained as current local measurement without the original complete fixture.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: - Because one visible-output token costs as much as **50 cache-read tokens** ($50 vs $1/MTok on Fable 5), compressing the always-cached instruction side is ~50x less valuable per token: a 60% cut of this repo's 2,738-token <RepoFile path="AGENTS.md">AGENTS.md</RepoFile> saves **≈$0.05/session (~1.4%)** — and carries rule-misread risk disproportionate to that.
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Withdrawn as current workload evidence: original complete session fixture and current usage receipts not reproduced; no universal thinking or visible-output ceiling.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: Per heavy modeled session (local baseline measurement, scaled): ~19 API calls, 5.5k uncached input, 85k cache-write, 1.17M cache-read, 27k output (55% thinking at max effort); ~$3.67/session, ~$22/heavy day at Fable 5 list prices. Dollar split: cache reads 32% / cache writes 29% / thinking 20% / visible output 17% / uncached input 2%.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: **Notation shootout** (same content): glyph DSL "↹ logs.csv ⊕ filter(level≥ERROR) ⇒ Σ summary ∴ top3 causes" = **42 tok**; plain English = **35 tok**; telegraphic ASCII "Read logs.csv. Filter level>=ERROR. Summarize. Top 3 causes." = **31 tok**. The DSL loses to plain prose by +20% and to telegraphic by +35%. A second sample measured DSL 36 / prose 40 / telegraphic 26: the DSL narrowly beat prose but lost to telegraphic by +38%. Across both samples, telegraphic ASCII used about 26–28% fewer tokens than the DSL.
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Reassessed under the mapped section; old number is not retained as current local measurement without the original complete fixture.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: **Math notation**: prose 37 tok; ASCII operators ("for all req in queue: if retries >= 3 and status != success -> mark failed") **24 tok (−35.1%)**; Unicode operators ("∀ req ∈ queue: retries ≥ 3 ∧ status ≠ success ⇒ mark failed") **38 tok (+2.7% vs prose)**. Unicode math costs MORE than full prose on this sample; ASCII is the only winning math notation.
numerical_claim_candidates.disposition: Reassessed under the mapped section; old number is not retained as current local measurement without the original complete fixture.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: **Wenyan / classical Chinese**: the original classical-Chinese rendering of "if all tests pass then commit" measured **9 tokens** versus **8 tokens** for the English phrase (net negative; original non-English text omitted). A longer rule measured 32 tokens in wenyan, 30 in plain English, and 25 in telegraphic English. Classical CJK ran **0.89–0.91 chars/token** here (at least one token per character). Characters are not tokens, and wenyan's measured savings are registral (extreme word-dropping), not tokenizer efficiency.

numerical_claim_candidates.text: - Anthropic runs exactly **two live tokenizer families**: official docs confirm Fable 5/Mythos 5 use the Opus-4.7 tokenizer, "roughly 30% more tokens" than older models. Locally the premium is **an ASCII/English tax**: ~0% on CJK/digits/emoji, +15.6% Python, +34% minified JSON, +59% English prose, **+132% SCREAMING_SNAKE**. Family equality is *exact*: Haiku 4.5 = Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.8 = Fable 5 on every probe. New-family membership: Opus 4.7 and later Opus models, Fable 5, Mythos 5, Mythos Preview, AND Claude Sonnet 5; old family is Sonnet 4.6 and earlier (incl. Haiku 4.5). All cross-family arbitrage numbers in this file are pinned to Sonnet 4.6/Haiku 4.5 targets.

Delta method: `tokens(payload) = count(payload as single user message) − overhead`, with overhead calibrated per model as `count("a") − 1` (6 on `claude-fable-5` and `claude-opus-4-8`; 7 on `claude-sonnet-4-6` and `claude-haiku-4-5`). Each payload is an n=1 sample; a second dataset with the same shape preserved the ordering but shifted magnitudes, so ranges are shown where relevant. Isolated 1–12 digit probes on Sonnet read a constant +1 over the `ceil(n/3)` law because of the single-message boundary; the law holds in-context for 20 eight-digit integers plus 19 newlines (79 Fable tokens = 20×3+19).

numerical_claim_candidates.text: - **Mechanism:** token complexity (arXiv 2503.01141): per problem there exists a threshold τ "such that for any prompt, the LLM gets the answer correct iff the token length is above τ" — cliff, not slope; success is predictable from token count alone with accuracy "above 90% for most models and benchmarks". Safe compression therefore requires ADAPTIVE allocation (more tokens to harder problems) — which is exactly what adaptive thinking + effort implements at platform level and what blanket "always be brief" cannot do. Information-loss side: moderate (2–6x) prompt compression "typically preserves or even enhances LLM performance… while extremely aggressive ratios (>10x) incur pronounced information loss and sometimes increase hallucination rates" (arXiv 2505.00019); compression modules "may discard key information such as negation cues (e.g., 'not'), factual disclaimers, time and location markers" (CompressionAttack, arXiv 2510.22963). CCoT's −27.69% GPT-3.5 math penalty and CoD's zero-shot collapse are output-side instances of the same threshold effect.
